title: Arrays, Strings, and the Array–Pointer Relationship
relevance: Arrays, array–pointer decay, and null-terminated C strings are core OA/SDE material because they drive memory layout reasoning, buffer safety, and low-level string manipulation.

phases.goal: Establish what C arrays and strings actually are in memory, including fixed size, contiguity, and the null-terminator convention.

must_hit.point: An array is a fixed-size, contiguous sequence of elements of the same type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines an array as identical elements laid out sequentially in one unbroken block.

must_hit.point: C does not store an array's length at runtime and does not perform bounds checking; out-of-range access is undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says length is not kept with the array and scores[10] just reads whatever is at that address.

must_hit.point: A C string is a char array that ends at the first null character '\0' (byte value 0), so storage must be at least one byte larger than the visible text.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the terminator convention and that "hello" needs room for six characters including '\0'.

must_hit.point: Historically array size must be known at compile time, indexing is zero-based, and uninitialized arrays contain garbage; C99 designated initializers can set specific indices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions compile-time size, zero-based indexing, garbage if uninitialized, and e.g. {[2]=42,[4]=99} yielding {0,0,42,0,99}.

probes: What is an array in C, and does the language know its length or check bounds at runtime?
How is a string represented in C, and what must every string's memory include beyond the visible characters?

hints.1: Think about raw contiguous storage, not a managed list or string object.
hints.2: Separate the array-as-block idea from the '\0'-terminated char-array convention for strings.
hints.3: Say: fixed contiguous same-type block; no runtime length/bounds; string ends at '\0' and needs that extra byte.

phases.goal: Explain array-to-pointer decay, the sizeof/& exceptions, function-parameter rewriting, subscript equivalence, and true 2D layout vs pointer types.

must_hit.point: In most expressions an array name decays to a pointer to its first element; exceptions include operand of sizeof, unary &, and a string literal used to initialize an array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states decay to &a[0] and names the sizeof, &, and string-literal-init exceptions.

must_hit.point: a[i] is defined as *(a + i); because addition is commutative, i[a] is valid C.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate equates subscripting with pointer arithmetic and notes i[a] works.

must_hit.point: Passing an array decays it; a parameter written int arr[] is rewritten to int *arr, so the callee gets an address copy and loses the array length.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the function receives a pointer, not the array, and length must be passed separately.

must_hit.point: A 2D array is physically one contiguous row-major strip (array of arrays) and decays to a pointer to an array, e.g. int (*p)[3], which differs from int *p[3] and int **p.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes row-major contiguity and correctly contrasts pointer-to-array, array-of-pointers, and pointer-to-pointer.

probes: Is an array a pointer? When does an array expression decay, and when does it not?
What actually happens to the type and length information when you pass an array to a function?
What does a true 2D array decay to, and how is that different from an array of pointers?

hints.1: Decay is a conversion of the array expression, not a change of what the array object is.
hints.2: Walk: expression decay rules → sizeof/& exceptions → parameter rewrite → row-major 2D decay type.
hints.3: Say: decays to &first except sizeof/&/literal-init; a[i]==*(a+i); int arr[] becomes int*; grid decays to int (*p)[width], not int**.

phases.goal: Compare the main design choices the material surfaces: array vs pointer identity, writable array strings vs read-only literals, memcpy vs memmove, and VLAs vs safer allocation.

must_hit.point: An array is not a pointer: for int a[5], sizeof(a) yields 20 (5 elements × 4 bytes), not the size of a pointer such as 8 on a 64-bit machine.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses the sizeof exception to prove array and pointer are different types.

must_hit.point: char s[] = "hello" copies into a writable array; char *p = "hello" points at a read-only string literal, so writing through p is unsafe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts stack/array copy (modifiable) with pointer-to-literal in read-only data.

must_hit.point: memcpy assumes non-overlapping regions; if source and destination might overlap, use memmove.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks memmove whenever overlap is possible and memcpy only when regions are disjoint.

must_hit.point: VLAs are convenient runtime-sized stack arrays but can blow the stack on large n; C11 made VLAs optional, and in C23 VLA types are mandatory while creating VLA objects on the stack remains optional.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate warns about stack overflow risk and states the C11/C23 optional-vs-mandatory nuance from the material.

probes: How would you prove that an array is not just a pointer?
When would you declare a string as char s[] versus char *p = "..."?
Why prefer memmove over memcpy in some copies, and what is the risk of VLAs?

hints.1: Compare what sizeof sees, where the bytes live, and who owns length/safety.
hints.2: Contrast object identity (array block vs pointer), mutability of literals, overlap rules, and stack limits.
hints.3: Say: sizeof(array) is the whole block; array form is writable, pointer-to-literal is not; memmove if overlap; VLAs are stack-risky and not always available as objects.

phases.goal: Apply decay, string conventions, and layout rules to concrete interview tasks and failure modes.

must_hit.point: Inside a function, sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) fails after decay: sizeof(arr) is the pointer size (e.g. 8), so with 4-byte ints the formula can evaluate to 2; always pass length separately.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects using sizeof on a parameter to recover length and requires an explicit length argument.

must_hit.point: char *s = "x"; s[0] = 'Y'; crashes because the literal lives in read-only data; use char s[] = "x" to get a modifiable copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names read-only literal storage and the array declaration fix.

must_hit.point: Map 2D (r, c) into a 1D array of WIDTH columns as r × WIDTH + c; in-place reverse walks left/right toward the center without touching '\0'; strlen counts until '\0' and excludes the terminator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives the row-major index formula, two-pointer reverse stopping before '\0', and strlen's terminator-excluding count.

must_hit.point: strcpy does not know dest size and can buffer-overflow; <string.h> supplies strlen, strcpy, strcmp (0 if equal), memcpy, memmove, and memset for manipulation because arrays cannot use = or ==.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate warns about strcpy overflow and names the library routines and strcmp's 0-for-equal result.

probes: Why is using sizeof to get an array's length inside a callee wrong, and what should you do instead?
Why does modifying a string through char *s = "x" crash, and how do you make it modifiable?
How do you flatten (r, c) into a 1D index, and how would you reverse a C string in place?

hints.1: Ask what type the function actually received, and where a string literal's bytes live.
hints.2: Tie decay-loss-of-length, read-only literals, row-major indexing, and terminator-aware walks together.
hints.3: Say: parameter is a pointer so sizeof is pointer-sized; write via char s[]; index = r*WIDTH+c; reverse before '\0'; don't trust strcpy's bounds.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: An array is the contiguous block; a pointer is only an address. Decay makes arrays masquerade as pointers in most expressions, but sizeof (and &) reveal they are different types—e.g. sizeof(int a[5]) is 20, not 8.
The array form allocates a writable copy (six bytes including '\0') you may modify; the pointer form points at a read-only literal, so writes can segfault. Prefer the array when mutation is required.
Both copy n bytes, but memcpy requires non-overlapping regions (overlap is undefined); memmove is safe when dest and src might overlap.

tradeoffs.topic: True 2D array vs array of pointers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: int grid[2][3] is one contiguous row-major block and decays to int (*p)[3]. int *p[3] is three separate pointers (e.g. for strings of different lengths); int **p is only a pointer to a pointer—not the same layout.

tradeoffs.topic: VLA convenience vs stack safety / standard support
tradeoffs.strong_answer: VLAs size the array at runtime on the stack, which is easy but can overflow on large or untrusted n. C11 made VLAs optional; C23 requires VLA types but leaving stack VLA objects optional for compilers.

gotchas.trap: Saying "an array is just a pointer."
gotchas.correction: False: they are different types. Decay converts an array expression to a pointer to the first element in most contexts, but sizeof on the array yields the full block size (e.g. 20 for int a[5]), not a pointer width.

gotchas.trap: Using sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) inside a function whose parameter is an array.
gotchas.correction: The parameter has already decayed to a pointer, so sizeof(arr) is the pointer size (e.g. 8), and with 4-byte elements that ratio can become 2. Always pass length as a separate parameter.
The literal is in read-only data; the write can segfault. Declare char s[] = "x" so a modifiable copy exists.

gotchas.trap: Trusting strcpy or memcpy without size/overlap discipline.
gotchas.correction: strcpy does not know dest capacity and can overflow. memcpy must not be used when regions overlap—use memmove if they might.

gotchas.trap: Declaring a large VLA from untrusted input.
gotchas.correction: VLAs live on the limited call stack; a large n can instantly stack-overflow. Treat VLAs as dangerous, and remember creating VLA objects is not required to be supported on all compilers.
